lessons.title: Storing a value and getting it back
lessons.intro: A price of $14.95 keeps coming up in your work, and you don't want to retype it. The calculator has ten memories, numbered 0 through 9. Store 14.95 in memory 3, wipe the display, then pull the value back — twice, to prove it stays put.

steps.explain: Key in the value you want to keep. It appears exactly as typed — the calculator doesn't format a number while you are still entering it.
STO followed by a digit copies the displayed value into that memory. Memory 3 now holds 14.95. Whatever was in there before is simply overwritten — there is no confirmation step.
Clear the display to zero. This is just to prove the next step really fetches the value from memory, not from the screen.
RCL followed by the digit brings the stored value back into the display, ready to use in a calculation.

Recall it again. Recalling only copies the value out — the memory still holds 14.95, so you can reuse it as many times as you like. When a memory has outlived its usefulness, overwrite it with zero (0 STO 3) and it reads as empty again.

lessons.answer: RCL 3 shows 14.95 every time. Storing overwrites a memory unconditionally, and recalling never empties it — the value stays until you store something else over it.

lessons.title: Running a total inside a memory with STO +
lessons.intro: You want a running total that lives in memory while the display stays free for other work. Start with 100 in memory 9, add 5 into it, then subtract 30 from it — all without ever disturbing what's on screen.

steps.explain: Store 100 in memory 9. Pressing STO finishes the number you were typing, so the display now shows it formatted to two decimals.

Key 5, then STO + 9. This adds the displayed 5 INTO memory 9, so the memory now holds 105 — but look at the screen: it still shows your 5. The addition happened entirely inside the memory; the screen never budged.
Recall memory 9 to see the result of the hidden addition: 100 + 5 = 105.

Now subtract. The order matters: the memory is always the left-hand side, so this computes memory minus display, 105 - 30 — not 30 - 105. The same rule holds for STO with divide and with the power key.
Recall memory 9 once more to confirm: 105 - 30 = 75.

lessons.answer: Memory 9 ends at 75.00. STO followed by +, -, ×, ÷, or y^x rewrites the memory as (memory op displayed value) in one short key sequence, while the display never moves — perfect for accumulating a total on the side.

lessons.title: Multiplying a whole list by 8 with the constant
lessons.intro: You need to multiply a whole list of numbers — 3, 7, and 45 — by the same 8. Instead of retyping × 8 every time, arm it once as a constant; after that, each new number needs only the = key.

steps.explain: Leave any worksheet and drop any half-finished calculation, so the constant starts from a clean slate.
Set up the first calculation as usual: 3 times 8. The display shows the raw 8 you just keyed — a number is shown exactly as typed while you are still entering it.
2ND K locks the '× 8' in as the constant. The = that follows does double duty: it finishes the first calculation, 3 × 8 = 24.
Here is the payoff. Key the next number and press = — the armed × 8 is applied automatically: 7 × 8 = 56.

And again: 45 × 8 = 360. The constant keeps working for any number of these number-then-= rounds. It stays armed until you set up a new operation and press 2ND K again — and if you have an ordinary calculation in progress, = finishes that first instead.

lessons.answer: 24.00, 56.00, 360.00 — one × 8, armed once with 2ND K, applied to every number you follow with =. The constant stays armed until you replace it with a new 2ND K or switch the calculator off, so a whole column of numbers costs one keystroke each.

lessons.title: Reusing the last answer with 2ND ANS
lessons.intro: Compute 3 + 1, then raise 2 to that result — without retyping the 4. The calculator quietly remembers the most recent result as the Last Answer, and 2ND ANS drops it into the middle of your next calculation.

steps.explain: A small calculation to make a result: 3 + 1 = 4. The = key is one of the moments the calculator saves its Last Answer, so ANS now holds 4.
Start the next calculation: 2 raised to a power. Pressing the operator key formats the pending 2 to 2.00 — and note that y^x does NOT touch the Last Answer, which still holds 4.
Recall the Last Answer as the exponent. The 4 from the first calculation reappears, sitting right where the exponent belongs.
Close the calculation: 2 to the 4th power is 16. This = also makes 16.00 the new Last Answer, ready for whatever comes next.

lessons.answer: 2^4 = 16.00, with the 4 supplied by 2ND ANS instead of your fingers. The Last Answer refreshes whenever =, ENTER, or CPT produces a value, so you can chain results between calculations — and even between worksheets — without rekeying them.
